newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Poland aims for full EU membership by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Poland aims for full EU membership by 2000.

text.p: Poland has set a date of 2000 for its full entry into the European Union, a move it sees as essential for its economic and political development, Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said on Thursday.
"We would like 2000 to be the year in which Poland achieves full membership of the Union," he said in a speech to the Royal Institute of International Affairs in The Hague.
"We are hopeful that accession to the European Union will become a boost to vibrant economic, social and cultural development in Poland and an additional guarantee of its international security."

Applicants to the EU from the former east bloc have been told that entry negotiations will begin six months after the end of next year's Inter-Governmental Conference (IGC), due to be wrapped up in June.

The Netherlands holds the rotating EU presidency in the first half of 1997 and Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok told Cimoszewicz on Wednesday he would try to conclude the IGC as soon as possible so talks could start in early 1998.

Cimoszewicz said he recognised the 2000 deadline imposed on Poland as "an obligation to intensify and accelerate reforms" adding he saw the process of integration with the Union as closely linked to Poland's hoped-for membership of NATO.
"Poland's admission to the North Atlantic Alliance is now ripe for definitive settlement. Our aim is to be a full member of the Alliance, enjoying its security guarantees," he said.

Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovenia are expected to be the first to be considered for membership of the now 16-member NATO alliance. The lengthy entry procedure could begin after a summit next year.
NATO's Partnership for Peace (PfP) agreement allowing for closer military co-operation, is regarded by many east European countries as a "waiting room" for full membership.

"We recognise the Partnership's significance as an additional European security framework...we expect our PfP activities to be of help in attaining our ultimate goal which is full membership of NATO," Cimoszewicz said.
Russia is strongly opposed to expansion of the NATO alliance, set up in the 1950s to counter Soviet military power.
Cimoszewicz said he expected a decision on Polish membership independently of objections from Russia or other agreements.
"Our position is that the expansion of the Alliance should be for Poland and the sixteen members to decide in a sovereign manner and irrespective of the stand taken by Russia," he said.
"The Russian objections to NATO enlargement seem to be grounded in the past; they fail to recognise the changes which have taken place in Europe."
